title: Chandler Reconstruction & Rebuild After Fire or Water Damage | Gold Water Fire | Phoenix, AZ
description: Reconstruction and rebuild in Chandler, AZ after fire or water damage. Drywall, flooring, cabinets, paint and structural repair from Gold Water Fire.
intro: The drying equipment is gone and the house is quieter now, but it is not a house you can live in normally. There is a bare slab where the flooring used to run, drywall cut off two feet up the wall in the hallway, a kitchen with the sink base pulled out and the plumbing capped. You have been managing around it, eating off paper plates, keeping the kids out of one room, telling yourself you will call somebody about the cabinets next week. That in-between stage is genuinely exhausting, and it is exhausting in a way nobody warns you about, because the emergency part is over and it feels like you should be past it by now.

sections.heading: The part after the damage is a construction job, not a cleanup job
sections.body: Mitigation and reconstruction are two different trades. Mitigation stops the loss and dries the structure: extraction, containment, air movers, removing materials that cannot be saved. Reconstruction is putting the house back: framing repairs, insulation, drywall hung and taped and textured to match, trim, doors, cabinets, countertops, tile and flooring, paint, and the electrical and plumbing work that goes with all of it. On a fire loss it can also mean roof and truss repair, replacing HVAC ductwork that pulled smoke through the house, and sealing framing that still carries odor. These are separate scopes of work with separate line items, and a lot of homeowners get stuck in the gap between them because the company that dried the house does not rebuild it. Gold Water Fire handles both sides, so the person who saw what was behind the wall is still involved when the wall goes back up. Our Construction Manager, Brandon Gurr, leads the reconstruction side, with Johnny as Reconstruction Team Lead running the crews on site.

sections.heading: What we run into in Chandler homes
sections.body: Chandler grew in distinct waves and the rebuild scope tends to follow the neighborhood. The older core around downtown and Arizona Avenue includes mid-century block and frame homes with original single-pane windows, plaster or thin drywall, and hardwood or sheet vinyl over slab. Matching those finishes takes sourcing, not a trip to the nearest big-box store. The large stretch of tract construction east of Alma School and out through Ocotillo, Fulton Ranch and the Price corridor went up largely in the 1990s and 2000s: slab-on-grade, engineered truss roofs, builder-grade oak or maple cabinets, and 20-inch tile that has been discontinued for years. When a supply line fails in a second-floor laundry room in one of those two-story plans, the water travels down through the floor system and you are rebuilding two levels, not one. Newer builds in south Chandler bring their own issue: tight, well-sealed envelopes that hold humidity and odor in after a loss instead of letting it clear. HOA design review is common across most of these subdivisions, and exterior repairs like stucco, roof tile and paint color usually need approval before work starts. We plan for that instead of getting surprised by it.

sections.heading: How the Valley calendar drives Chandler losses
sections.body: Two seasons produce most of the reconstruction work here. Monsoon season, roughly July through September, brings microbursts that lift roof tile and drive rain sideways into fascia, valleys and skylights, and Chandler's flat terrain and heavy caliche layer mean stormwater sits rather than soaks, so yard flooding backs up against slabs and gets in at the threshold. The second is plain heat. Attic temperatures in a Chandler summer are brutal on plastic supply lines, water heater tank seams and washing machine hoses, and a failure while nobody is home means hours of water across the slab and up into the drywall and cabinet toe kicks. Winter is quieter, but that is when the seasonal-resident and vacant-home losses show up, discovered days or weeks later. On any of these, the useful question for the rebuild is not just what got wet, but how far the water wicked up the drywall and whether the cabinet boxes and MDF baseboards swelled. Particleboard cabinet bottoms and paper-faced drywall do not recover; solid wood face frames often do.

sections.heading: Working the scope and the insurance paperwork together
sections.body: Most rebuilds are paid through a property claim, and the claim moves on documentation. That means photos before demo, a written scope with line items, and matching what was actually there (the tile, the cabinet profile, the paint sheen) instead of a vague allowance. Where an adjuster's estimate misses something, the fix is not arguing, it is showing the condition with evidence. We write the scope, communicate with your adjuster, and keep you copied so you are never guessing where things stand. Kristine in our office handles the coordination and paperwork side, and Brooke schedules the water and mitigation work when both phases are in play. Our AZ ROC license is #264344, KB-2. If you want to see the front half of the process, read about water damage restoration or fire damage restoration, or the full reconstruction and rebuild scope. Our office is on E Willis Rd in Chandler, so this is not a service area we drive across town to reach. It is where we work from.

faqs.q: Can you do the rebuild if another company dried out my house?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly pick up reconstruction after another company handled the mitigation. We will want to see their drying documentation and moisture readings so we know the structure was actually dry before anything gets closed up, and we will walk the house with you to write the rebuild scope from current conditions.

faqs.q: Will you match my existing tile and cabinets if they were discontinued?
faqs.a: Often we can get close, and sometimes we can get exact by sourcing discontinued stock. Where a true match is not available, we talk through options before ordering, including where it makes more sense to continue a new material to a natural break line, like a doorway or a change in room, so the repair does not read as a patch.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval before you start?
faqs.a: For interior work, usually not. For anything visible from the street in most Chandler subdivisions (stucco, exterior paint, roof tile, windows), the HOA design review typically needs to sign off first. Tell us your community early and we will build that step into the schedule instead of stopping work halfway through.

faqs.q: How long will my Chandler home be torn up?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the scope, material lead times and how quickly the claim is approved, so we will not guess at a number before we have seen it. What we will do is give you a written schedule once the scope is set, and tell you plainly when something slips and why.

cta.heading: Let someone else carry the rebuild from here
cta.body: You have already gotten through the worst part of this. Putting the house back is a construction project with permits, materials, trades and a claim attached, and it is a reasonable thing to hand off. Call Gold Water Fire at (480) 999-3339 or email Help@goldwaterfire.com, and we will come look at what is left and tell you straight what it takes to finish it.
